blocks.alt: The Adecco Group prototyping framework shown across devices

blocks.text: The brief assumed the answer was a tool

The Adecco Group wanted teams to test ideas earlier and bring promising concepts to market faster. The initial brief asked me to identify a prototyping platform that could use the existing React design system and make high-fidelity validation easier.

I was new to the organisation and did not yet know what teams wanted to test, how prototypes fitted into delivery or why existing tools were not enough. Choosing software before answering those questions would have turned a product decision into a feature comparison.

items: What decision should this prototype support?
Who needs to understand or test it?
How much time and specialist help are available?
What level of realism would change the answer?

blocks.label: Reframed brief
blocks.text: Define how teams should choose and use prototypes, then decide which tools belong in that system.
Teams needed a way to choose, not another default

I surveyed designers, developers, product managers, product owners and business partners, then facilitated a workshop with 13 cross-functional participants. The research showed that people struggled before they reached the tool itself.

items: Purpose
Teams were unclear about what a prototype needed to prove.
Audience
The person reviewing a concept often needed something different from the person testing it.
Fidelity
People overbuilt prototypes because they lacked guidance on how realistic they needed to be.
Support
Someone with an idea did not always have access to a designer or developer.
Sometimes I have an idea, but I do not have anybody to help me flesh it out.
If I put something together, who is the best person to show it to?

blocks.text: An audit of the existing design-system resources confirmed a gap at the high-fidelity end, but the research also showed why one universal tool would fail. Different teams needed different balances of speed, control, data and technical support.

blocks.alt: Audit of existing prototyping tools plotted by fidelity and maturity
blocks.caption: The audit made the high-fidelity gap visible, while the research explained why adding one tool would not solve every use case.

blocks.text: The first technical assumption was wrong

I evaluated Bubble and Power Apps because both appeared capable of supporting more realistic prototypes. Under time pressure and without engineering support, I initially assumed we could integrate the React component library into either environment.

Deeper testing and conversations with the vendors proved otherwise. Bubble required the components to be rebuilt, while Power Apps could apply styling but could not consume the custom React components. The proposed shortcut between prototype and production did not exist.

rows: Reuse the React library in Bubble
Components would need to be recreated from scratch
Integrate custom components in Power Apps
The platform supported styling, not direct React integration
Select one high-fidelity platform
The tools served different audiences and constraints
Reduce the gap to production automatically
Teams still needed to choose fidelity and effort deliberately

blocks.text: I shared the mistake with stakeholders and reframed the recommendation. This is the central decision in the case: technical investigation changed the strategy rather than being used to justify the original choice.

blocks.alt: Research and evaluation of Bubble and Power Apps
blocks.caption: The tool evaluation tested integration, onboarding effort and suitability rather than comparing feature lists alone.

blocks.text: I reframed the tools around different jobs
Instead of presenting a winner, I mapped each option to the situations where it added value and made its limitations explicit.

rows: Existing design tools
How can I communicate an interface or flow quickly?
Use for low and medium fidelity without unnecessary setup
Power Apps
How can I test an internal concept with data?
Use its dataset connections without depending on custom React components
Bubble
How can I create an interactive flow without engineering?
Use selectively for interactive concepts; do not treat it as the default
Coded prototype
When does production-like behaviour matter?
Use when the decision justifies engineering effort

blocks.text: The decision matrix asked about audience, available time, required fidelity and the question being tested. This helped teams avoid both extremes: skipping validation because the process felt inaccessible, or building a production-like prototype before it was useful.

items: Define the decision
Choose the audience
Select the fidelity
Match the tool

blocks.text: The framework made the decision reusable

I turned the research and tool evaluation into a self-service framework on the internal design-system site. It combined the decision matrix with tool guidance, examples and onboarding so people could begin without waiting for a specialist to interpret the options.

blocks.alt: Published prototyping framework on The Adecco Group’s design-system site
blocks.caption: The published framework connected the decision process to practical guidance for each tool.

blocks.text: I also presented the work at The Adecco Group’s design conference in Berlin. The talk made the reasoning available to employees, contractors and partner organisations, but the case does not treat attendance as proof of lasting adoption.

blocks.alt: Presenting the prototyping framework at The Adecco Group’s design conference in Berlin
blocks.caption: The conference introduced the research, trade-offs and decision framework to a wider internal audience.

blocks.alt: Audience at The Adecco Group’s design conference presentation
blocks.caption: The presentation extended the framework beyond the immediate project team.

blocks.text: Early evidence, not proof at scale

Twenty people responded to the initial satisfaction measure, and 15 gave the framework the highest rating, producing a 75% top-rating result. In the first 30 days, 43% of the target audience completed onboarding and one team used the guidance in a project.

items: Satisfaction
15 of 20 respondents gave the framework the highest rating.
Onboarding
43% of the target audience onboarded during the first month.
Use
One team applied the framework to a project in the first 30 days.

blocks.text: These results indicate that the framework was understandable and relevant at launch. They do not yet demonstrate company-wide behaviour change or the long-term effect on product delivery.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.text: The strongest outcome was not selecting a tool. It was giving teams a way to choose proportionately, including when the right answer was a simpler prototype.
